title: Beauty From Chaos
caption: The merging galaxy NGC 34, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 34 · constellation Cetus · about 270 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, A. Adamo et al.

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: NGC 34 looks less like a galaxy than a glowing creature from the deep ocean. Its outer region seems almost translucent, pricked with stars and odd wispy tendrils, around a bright center. The galaxy lies in the constellation Cetus (The Sea Monster), about 270 million light-years away.

Its strange look comes from its history. A few million years ago there were two spiral galaxies heading straight for each other. When they collided, their spiral arms and intricate patterns were permanently disrupted.

The bright center is a product of that merger, which triggered a burst of new star formation and made the surrounding gas glow. As the two galaxies keep blending into one, NGC 34 will lose any distinct shape and become a peculiar galaxy. Collisions between galaxies are rare in the vastness of space, but they can be common in huge clusters that contain hundreds or even thousands of galaxies.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.60 x 2.53 arcminutes) and distance (270 million light years), the frame spans roughly 204,000 × 199,000 light-years. Its light set out about 270 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 34 in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The color mapping isn't published.
filters: 665 nm · Optical H-alpha + N II (Hubble WFC3)
understand.eye: Some of these filters record light the eye cannot see, and the galaxy's faint outer tendrils would be invisible without Hubble.

explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 34 through five filters, from ultraviolet to near-infrared light, including one that picks up glowing hydrogen. The observations are credited to A. Adamo and colleagues.
alt: A galaxy with a bright center surrounded by a faint, almost translucent outer region with scattered stars and wispy tendrils.
